title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 25–26
description: Curated B2 vocabulary for describing towns and city facilities, urban challenges, animal and plant anatomy, and verbs for natural processes.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Complete illustrated study pages, city facilities and problem tables, nature diagrams, lexical contrasts, usage notes, exercises and answer-key entries reviewed for relevant learning targets.
audit.pronunciation: Selected broad British IPA for familiar single words and short expressions; longer or uncertain pronunciations omit IPA rather than assert an unreliable transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: English only, except Brazilian Portuguese glosses in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual source and answer-key comparison, language and IPA review, audio-target checks and offline JSON structural validation. No live VocabLab import or browser audio/recognition testing was performed.
audit.limitations: No prerecorded audio is bundled. Live web-browser TTS, speech recognition and app runtime compatibility were not tested.

units.title: Unit 25 — Towns
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 56–57 (PDF pages 57–58).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe cities accurately using city-centre, district, suburb, outskirts and other urban vocabulary.
Talk about public services, cultural venues, accommodation, transport and local facilities.
Explain urban challenges such as traffic jams, pollution, vandalism, slums and overcrowding.
Use appropriate descriptive adjectives and collocations such as within walking distance, put on an exhibition and open spaces.

items.example: The city offers museums, universities and regular concerts.
items.note: City often suggests a larger urban settlement with a wide range of facilities; legal definitions differ.

items.example: She moved from a village to a busy market town.
items.note: Town usually refers to a settlement smaller than a city; the boundaries are not universal.

items.example: The market sells fresh vegetables and flowers every Saturday.
items.note: A place where several traders sell goods; the source describes two markets in Cork.

items.example: The coastal metropolis attracts people from across the region.
items.note: A very large or important city; the source calls Cork a major metropolis of southern Ireland.

items.example: The town has a population of roughly eighty thousand.
items.note: Common pattern: a population of + number.

items.example: The main business centre is close to the station.
items.note: An area where many offices and businesses are located; not necessarily a single building.

items.example: A new shopping centre opened near the railway station.
items.note: British English; in American English shopping mall or mall is common for a large enclosed complex.

items.example: Two narrow channels separate the island from the riverbank.
items.note: Here a stretch of water, not a television channel or communication channel.

items.example: She lives in a quiet suburb west of the centre.
items.note: A residential area outside or near the central part of a city; it need not be deprived or rural.

items.example: Buses tend to be crowded at the end of the working day.
items.note: Use tend to + infinitive to describe what commonly happens; source pattern: tend to be overcrowded.

items.pt: a uma distância que se pode percorrer a pé
items.example: The art gallery is within walking distance of our hotel.
items.note: Useful collocation with of: within walking distance of the centre.

items.example: Buses become overcrowded during the morning rush hour.
items.note: Too many people in a place or vehicle; stronger than crowded.

items.pt: sistema de trânsito de mão única
items.example: Visitors sometimes find the one-way traffic system confusing.
items.note: A system of streets in which traffic may travel in only one direction along specified roads.

items.pt: sistema de trânsito; organização do tráfego
items.example: The city redesigned its traffic system to reduce delays.
items.note: How movement of road traffic is organised.

items.example: The church steeple can be seen from the river.
items.note: A tall, often pointed structure rising above a church.

items.example: The old bell tower rings every hour.
items.note: A tower containing one or more bells.

items.example: The library stands on the site of an old factory.
items.note: Site here means a particular place where a building once stood.

items.example: The army tried to besiege the fortified town.
items.note: A formal historical verb for surrounding a place to cut off supplies; past besieged.

items.example: The city cathedral is famous for its stained-glass windows.
items.note: A principal church containing a bishop's official seat.

items.example: An imposing stone building dominates the square.
items.note: Large or impressive in a way that commands attention.

items.example: The cathedral was built in the Gothic style.
items.note: A style of architecture commonly associated with pointed arches and medieval cathedrals.

items.pt: atender às necessidades de; servir a
items.example: The museum caters for visitors of all ages.
items.note: British pattern: cater for a group; American English often uses cater to.

items.example: The street market has a lively atmosphere on weekends.
items.note: A common pairing for places full of energy, movement and conversation.

items.example: The narrow streets give the old quarter its charm.
items.note: An attractive quality that makes a place pleasant or memorable.

items.example: The town has excellent sports and arts facilities.
items.note: Facilities are equipment, buildings or services provided for a particular purpose.

items.example: The local history museum is well worth a visit.
items.note: Well worth + noun or -ing: well worth visiting, not well worth to visit.

items.example: The gallery will put on an exhibition of local photography.
items.note: Put on means organise or present a public event, performance or exhibition.

items.example: The gallery is known for adventurous contemporary displays.
items.note: Here describes imaginative or experimental art, rather than someone enjoying physical risk.

items.example: The museum displays work by contemporary artists.
items.note: Contemporary here means of the present or relatively recent period.

items.example: The riverside district has become a fashionable place to live.
items.note: Describes a desirable, stylish or popular place; can suggest high property prices.

items.example: The residential district is quiet after dark.
items.note: An area containing mainly homes rather than shops or factories.

items.example: Their flat overlooks the harbour.
items.note: In descriptions of buildings it means have a view of; another sense is fail to notice.

items.example: Fishing boats returned to the harbour before dusk.
items.note: British spelling harbour; American harbor; sheltered coastal place for vessels.

items.example: A new industrial park is being built on the outskirts of town.
items.note: Normally plural: on the outskirts of a city or town, not on the outskirt.

items.example: Children learn to swim at the public swimming pool.
items.note: A purpose-built pool for swimming, often part of a sports centre.

items.example: The sports centre has a gym and several indoor courts.
items.note: British spelling centre; American center.

items.example: The resort has an eighteen-hole golf course.
items.note: An area designed for the sport of golf.

items.example: We booked a tennis court for Saturday morning.
items.note: Court is the playing area for tennis and several other sports.

items.example: The school has a football pitch behind the main building.
items.note: Pitch is common in British English for the playing surface; American English often says soccer field.

items.example: The new skating rink is busy in winter.
items.note: A prepared area for skating; specify ice rink when ice is important.

items.example: The theatre stages plays by local writers.
items.note: British spelling theatre; American theater.

items.example: The opera house hosts performances throughout the season.
items.note: A venue designed or used for opera performances.

items.example: The orchestra performs at the concert hall each month.
items.note: A purpose-built venue for live musical performances.

items.pt: estação de rádio; emissora de rádio
items.example: A local radio station broadcasts community news.
items.note: A broadcaster that transmits radio programmes.

items.example: The art gallery displays paintings by regional artists.
items.note: A building or space for displaying art; often stages exhibitions.

items.example: The museum has a collection of historic maps.
items.note: An institution that collects, preserves or displays objects of interest.

items.example: She attends a college offering professional qualifications.
items.note: In British English often further education or a component of a university; meanings vary across countries.

items.example: The university attracts students from other regions.
items.note: An institution of higher education and research.

items.example: You can borrow books from the public library.
items.note: Place where books and other resources are available to read or borrow.

items.example: The adult education centre offers evening language classes.
items.note: A place where adults take academic, practical or recreational courses.

items.example: We had lunch at a small restaurant near the market.
items.note: A place where meals are prepared and served.

items.pt: restaurante de comida para viagem; comida para levar
items.example: We bought dinner from the Chinese take-away.
items.note: British spelling for food purchased to eat elsewhere or the shop selling it; American takeout.

items.example: The hotel is within walking distance of the station.
items.note: Accommodation offering rooms, often with additional services.

items.example: They stayed at a family-run bed and breakfast.
items.note: Often abbreviated B&B; accommodation with breakfast included.

items.example: The hikers spent the night in a youth hostel.
items.note: Budget accommodation, often with shared rooms; not necessarily restricted to young travellers.

items.example: They went to a club to dance after the concert.
items.note: In this unit it can refer to a nightlife venue; club has other meanings too.

items.example: The bus service runs every fifteen minutes.
items.note: Service means the organised provision and frequency of buses.

items.example: There is a taxi rank outside the station.
items.note: British English; American English taxi stand.

items.example: Car hire is available at the airport.
items.note: British English; American English car rental.

items.example: The multi-storey car park is close to the shops.
items.note: British English; American English parking lot or parking garage depending on type.

items.example: The parking meter accepts card payments.
items.note: A device used to pay for parking in a designated space.

items.pt: centro de saúde; unidade de atendimento de saúde
items.example: The new health centre provides general medical appointments.
items.note: British term for a local healthcare facility.

items.example: The law courts are beside the civic square.
items.note: Courts are places where legal cases are heard; not sports courts in this context.

items.pt: cartório de registro civil; órgão de registro civil
items.example: They arranged a civil wedding at the registry office.
items.note: In the UK a local office handling births, marriages and deaths; procedures vary elsewhere.

items.example: The citizens' advice bureau can help residents understand their rights.
items.note: A traditional British term for a free advice service; present-day UK organisations often use the name Citizens Advice.

items.example: He visited the job centre to ask about vacancies.
items.note: A place offering employment-related services; the UK also uses the official name Jobcentre Plus.

items.example: The department store sells clothing, cosmetics and home goods.
items.note: A large shop organised into sections selling different types of products.

items.example: You can buy the medicine at the chemist's.
items.note: British term for a pharmacy; the apostrophe is conventional in this shop meaning.

items.example: We bought compost at the garden centre.
items.note: A retail business selling plants and gardening equipment.

items.example: She reported the stolen bicycle at the police station.
items.note: A building used by police officers to conduct their work.

items.example: The council meets in the town hall.
items.note: The municipal administration building; city hall is also used, especially for cities.

items.example: An estate agent showed us several flats.
items.note: British English; American English real estate agent.

items.example: A new housing estate has been built north of the river.
items.note: A planned group of houses or flats; connotation varies by region.

items.example: Several small manufacturers operate from the industrial estate.
items.note: An area planned for factories, warehouses and industrial businesses.

items.example: High housing costs can contribute to poverty in urban areas.
items.note: Lack of sufficient income or resources for basic needs; the source links poverty to poor housing.

items.example: Damaging public property is an act of vandalism.
items.note: In the city-problems table, property refers to buildings and possessions, not personal traits.

items.example: A traffic jam delayed the buses for nearly an hour.
items.note: Vehicles move very slowly or stop because roads are overcrowded.

items.pt: pessoa que se desloca regularmente para o trabalho ou estudo
items.example: Commuters were delayed by the morning traffic jam.
items.note: Someone who regularly travels between home and work or education.

items.example: Trains are packed during the evening rush hour.
items.note: The part of the day when travel demand is highest.

items.pt: área urbana de moradias muito precárias; favela, dependendo do contexto
items.example: The city launched a programme to improve housing in the slum.
items.note: A deprived urban area with poor-quality housing; may be pejorative, so use carefully.

items.example: The park has suffered repeated acts of vandalism.
items.note: Deliberate, unjustified damage to property.

items.example: Overcrowding has put pressure on local housing and transport.
items.note: Condition in which too many people occupy a space.

items.example: Air pollution worsened when road traffic increased.
items.note: The contamination of the environment; uncountable in this sense.

items.example: Residents noticed a deterioration in air quality.
items.note: A process of becoming worse; common pattern deterioration in or of.

items.example: A reliable public transport system can ease congestion.
items.note: Buses, trains and other transport services available to the public.

items.example: Stricter standards could reduce traffic emissions.
items.note: Exhaust gases and particles produced by road traffic; highlighted in the exercises.

items.example: The old town has picturesque streets and stone houses.
items.note: Very attractive, especially in a way that could suit a picture.

items.example: The town is known for its historic market square.
items.note: Historic means important in history; historical more broadly means related to history.

items.example: The renovated library has a spacious reading room.
items.note: Containing plenty of room; opposite cramped.

items.example: The elegant buildings line a quiet avenue.
items.note: Stylish and pleasing in appearance.

items.example: The cathedral is a magnificent example of Gothic architecture.
items.note: Exceptionally impressive or beautiful.

items.example: The city centre is lively on Friday evenings.
items.note: Full of activity, energy and people.

items.example: The shopping streets were deserted early on Sunday.
items.note: Almost empty of people, not necessarily geographically a desert.

items.example: We enjoyed the bustling market near the harbour.
items.note: Busy, lively and full of activity.

items.example: The concert hall was packed with spectators.
items.note: Extremely full; common pattern packed with people.

items.example: The abandoned alley was filthy after the storm.
items.note: Much stronger than dirty; can sound critical.

items.example: The council plans to renovate a run-down neighbourhood.
items.note: In poor physical condition owing to neglect; usually hyphenated before a noun.

items.example: The city has many open spaces where residents can relax.
items.note: Use open spaces, not open places, for parks and undeveloped urban areas.

sectionsChecked: A: Describing a city and vocabulary from the Cork description
B: Facilities including sport, culture, education, accommodation, transport and services

units.title: Unit 26 — The natural world
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 58–59 (PDF pages 59–60).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Identify common animal body parts and bird features, including beaks, wings, feathers, paws, claws, hooves and horns.
Name the parts of flowers and trees and distinguish boughs, branches, twigs, bark and roots.
Recognise animals and creatures pictured in the unit and the unusual plural of deer.
Use precise natural-world verbs and patterns: flower or blossom, pick flowers, lay eggs, grow, breed and pick up.

items.example: The bird spread its wings before taking off.
items.note: Wings are body parts used by birds, bats and many insects to fly.

items.example: The parrot uses its beak to break open seeds.
items.note: The hard mouthpart of a bird; often called a bill in certain species.

items.example: The bird laid an egg in its nest.
items.note: Many birds reproduce by laying eggs; irregular past of lay is laid.

items.example: A pair of birds built a nest in the tree.
items.note: A structure in which birds and some other animals keep eggs or young.

items.example: A colourful feather fell from the bird's wing.
items.note: A bird's light body covering; feathers collectively form plumage.

items.example: A cat uses its whiskers to sense objects nearby.
items.note: Often plural whiskers when referring to long sensitive hairs near a cat's nose.

items.example: The fox has thick fur during winter.
items.note: Soft hair covering the body of many mammals; normally uncountable.

items.example: The dog wagged its tail when it saw us.
items.note: The body part extending from the back of an animal.

items.example: The cat lifted one paw to clean its face.
items.note: A soft foot with pads and often claws, especially on cats or dogs.

items.example: The kitten caught the toy with its claws.
items.note: A sharp curved nail on an animal's foot; distinct from an entire paw.

items.example: The horse has a long dark mane.
items.note: Long hair along the neck of a horse or around a lion's head.

items.example: The young goat already has small horns.
items.note: A hard pointed growth on the head of certain animals.

items.example: The vet checked the horse's injured hoof.
items.note: The hard covering of the foot of an animal such as a horse; plural hooves, also hoofs.

items.example: The flower has five bright red petals.
items.note: One of the usually colourful parts surrounding the centre of a flower.

items.example: Bees carry pollen between flowers.
items.note: Fine powder made by seed plants; usually uncountable.

items.example: The rosebud will open in a few days.
items.note: An undeveloped flower or new growth on a plant.

items.example: Take care because this plant has sharp thorns.
items.note: A pointed growth on a plant; a thorn may prick the skin.

items.example: A yellow leaf fell onto the path.
items.note: Irregular plural leaves, not leafs.

items.example: Cut the flower stem at an angle before putting it in water.
items.note: The main supporting part of a small plant or the stalk of a flower.

items.example: A large bough fell during the storm.
items.note: A large or main tree branch; bough rhymes with now.

items.example: A bird landed on a branch above the path.
items.note: A woody limb growing out from a tree trunk; usually larger than a twig.

items.example: They collected dry twigs to start the fire.
items.note: A small, thin branch, often from the end of a bigger branch.

items.example: The bark of this tree is rough and dark.
items.note: The outer covering of a tree; bark is also a verb meaning a dog's sound.

items.example: The oak has a wide trunk and spreading branches.
items.note: The main upright woody stem of a tree.

items.example: The roots absorb water from the soil.
items.note: A plant part, often underground, that anchors the plant and takes in water and nutrients.

items.example: A small frog jumped into the pond.
items.note: An amphibian that usually has long hind legs and jumps or swims.

items.example: The whale surfaced near the boat.
items.note: A large marine mammal; unlike fish, whales breathe air.

items.example: The shark swam slowly past the reef.
items.note: A large predatory fish in many species; contrasts with the mammal whale.

items.example: A bat flew above the garden at dusk.
items.note: A flying mammal, not a bird; the word also means a sports bat.

items.example: A worm moved through the damp soil.
items.note: A long soft-bodied invertebrate; the pictured example resembles an earthworm.

items.example: We saw three deer at the edge of the forest.
items.note: Singular and plural are both deer: one deer, several deer.

items.example: An owl called from the woods after sunset.
items.note: A bird of prey often active at night.

items.example: A fox crossed the lane near our house.
items.note: A wild mammal related to dogs, often with a bushy tail.

items.example: The snail moved across the wet stone.
items.note: A slow-moving mollusc often carrying a spiral shell.

items.example: A crab hid beneath a rock by the shore.
items.note: A crustacean with a hard shell and claws; not a marine mammal.

items.example: A pigeon landed on the balcony.
items.note: A common bird found in towns and the countryside.

items.example: The peacock spread its colourful tail feathers.
items.note: Strictly the male of a peafowl; peahen is the female.

items.example: A seal rested on the rocks near the beach.
items.note: A marine mammal, not a fish; seal has several unrelated noun and verb meanings.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: The cherry trees flower in early spring.
items.note: Verb meaning produce flowers; also a noun meaning a flower.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: The apple trees blossom when the weather becomes warmer.
items.note: Near synonym for flower as a verb; also refers to flowers on fruit trees.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: We picked flowers to decorate the table.
items.note: Pick means remove something growing from a plant; not pick up flowers in this meaning.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: We often pick fruit from the orchard in autumn.
items.note: Use pick, not pick up, when taking growing fruit off a tree or plant.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: The hens lay eggs in a sheltered nesting area.
items.note: Irregular verb lay–laid–laid; do not confuse with lie–lay–lain.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: Bees collect pollen as they visit different flowers.
items.note: A useful verb–noun combination; pollen can be carried between flowers.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: Bees make honey from nectar gathered at flowers.
items.note: Pollen is collected too, but honey is made primarily from nectar.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: These wild flowers grow well in sandy soil.
items.note: Intransitive grow has no direct object: plants grow quickly.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: We grow tomatoes in pots on the balcony.
items.note: Transitive grow takes an object: people grow tomatoes or other plants.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: These birds breed near the coast each summer.
items.note: Intransitive use describes animal reproduction; past and participle bred.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: Her family breeds horses on a small farm.
items.note: Transitive use means keep animals so that they reproduce; past bred.

items.section: D · Nature processes and verb patterns
items.example: He picked up the keys that had fallen onto the floor.
items.note: Pick up means lift something from where it fell or was placed, not harvest it from a plant.

items.example: Bees collect nectar from flowers to produce honey.
items.note: A sugary liquid produced by flowers; appears in exercise 26.1.

items.example: A large oak stands near the entrance to the park.
items.note: A type of tree; appears among the plant vocabulary in exercise 26.2.

items.example: The willow grows beside the stream.
items.note: A tree often found near water; appears in exercise 26.2.

items.example: A national emblem can be an animal, plant or other representative symbol.
items.note: The unit exercise discusses the tulip and maple leaf as national emblems.

items.example: She picked fresh herbs for the evening meal.
items.note: Used in the matching exercise; British English pronounces the initial h.

items.example: The maple leaf is widely recognised as a symbol of Canada.
items.note: The source exercise mentions the maple leaf as a national emblem.

items.pt: fruto do mar com concha ou carapaça
items.example: Crabs and lobsters are types of shellfish.
items.note: A broad culinary term for aquatic crustaceans and molluscs; appears in the answer key.
